title: To Cut Electricity Bills, Britain Needs to Use More, Not Less
gist: BCG argues Britain's high electricity bills stem from taxes/levies and a fixed-cost grid built for shrinking demand, not from gas or generation costs, and that the fastest fix is to grow demand rather than shrink it -- specifically by bringing 14GW of grid-positive data centre load onto the system by 2035 alongside a ~£174/year package of near-term cost reallocation.

insights.claim: British domestic electricity prices are the fourth highest in the EU14+GB peer group and non-domestic prices are the highest, while domestic gas prices are the lowest in the group -- Britain's high energy costs are an electricity-specific problem, not a broad energy-cost problem.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/maurice-berns
insights.so_what: Policy and investment attention aimed at gas supply won't fix UK affordability; the lever is electricity market design and network cost recovery specifically.
insights.locator: Executive Summary

insights.claim: Britain's electricity-to-gas price ratio is 4.2x versus a 2.7x peer median (around 60% higher), and BCG's own model shows this ratio rising a further one-fifth by 2035.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/maurice-berns
insights.so_what: The electrification cost penalty (relative to gas) is set to widen, working against electrification of heat and transport unless policy intervenes.
insights.locator: Executive Summary

insights.claim: Britain's underlying cost of generating and delivering electricity is level with most European peers; the premium comes from taxes/levies on bills and from gas setting electricity prices more often, not from higher production costs -- the Netherlands and Austria have similar underlying network/supply costs (24p/kWh) but lower net levies, while France and Spain have similar levies but gas rarely sets their prices because of nuclear and renewables.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/maurice-berns
insights.so_what: The fix is a policy/market-design problem (levy allocation, merit-order exposure), not a supply-side or generation-cost problem -- reframes where reform effort should go.
insights.locator: Context: Electricity Costs Drive Britain's High Energy Bills

insights.claim: Further North Sea gas exploration is unlikely to meaningfully lower British bills because British gas prices are set by the wider interconnected European gas market rather than domestic output, and UK gas production is already less than half of domestic demand and declining.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/maurice-berns
insights.so_what: Investors and policymakers betting on domestic gas supply as a bill-relief lever are targeting the wrong variable; any North Sea case has to rest on security-of-supply or fiscal grounds, not consumer prices.
insights.quote: British gas prices are set by the wider, interconnected European gas market, not by how much gas Britain itself produces.
insights.locator: Context: Electricity Costs Drive Britain's High Energy Bills

themes.theme: Bill vs. System Cost Gap and the Negative Demand Spiral

insights.claim: The gap between what households are billed and the true underlying system cost of building and running Britain's grid has more than tripled since 2015, partly because the domestic tariff's network charge (9.1 p/kWh) is roughly 1.75x the system-wide average network cost (5.2 p/kWh), since households connect at low voltage and spread fixed costs over smaller volumes.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/maurice-berns
insights.so_what: Bills overstate the true cost of the system -- large flexible consumers (like data centres) connecting at higher voltage can add demand at meaningfully lower marginal system cost than households.
insights.locator: Context: Electricity Costs Drive Britain's High Energy Bills

insights.claim: An 11% fall in total GB electricity demand since 2015 explains 39% of the rise in electricity system cost -- more than any other single factor -- evidencing a self-reinforcing spiral where falling demand raises the unit cost of Britain's largely fixed grid infrastructure.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/maurice-berns
insights.so_what: Demand decline, not gas or renewables build-out, is the single biggest driver of rising system costs -- reversing that decline is the highest-leverage lever available.
insights.locator: Context: Electricity Costs Drive Britain's High Energy Bills

insights.claim: For consumer bills specifically (distinct from system cost), wholesale price rises explain 38% and network/policy costs explain 45% of the 2015-24 increase -- gas is a real but partial driver, not the sole cause of rising bills.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/maurice-berns
insights.so_what: Narratives that blame gas alone for UK bill pain are only about a third correct -- network and policy costs are now the larger driver and the one policy can act on directly.
insights.locator: Executive Summary

insights.claim: Rooftop solar-plus-battery adoption is a rational individual response to high bills, but the network fixed costs it avoids do not disappear -- they shift onto everyone else, disproportionately renters and households without capital to opt out, adding an estimated £12-25/year to a typical bill by 2035 depending on battery uptake.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/maurice-berns
insights.so_what: Rising self-generation adoption is a quiet regressive tax on non-adopters -- a distributional risk for policymakers and a demand-side headwind for grid economics.
insights.quote: the fixed costs in the system do not disappear – they move onto everyone else, and disproportionately onto renters and households without the capital to opt out.
insights.locator: Vision of the Future: Higher Fixed Costs Driving Rising Bills

insights.claim: Britain is caught in a negative demand/price spiral in which high bills suppress electricity demand, which raises the unit cost of the fixed-cost grid, pushing bills higher still -- breaking or reversing this spiral is the central policy objective of the report.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/maurice-berns
insights.so_what: Frames the entire UK power-affordability debate as a demand problem rather than a supply or generation-mix problem -- the throughline for every policy lever the report proposes.
insights.quote: bills suppress demand, which in turn raises unit costs given the high fixed-cost base.
insights.locator: Vision of the Future: Higher Fixed Costs Driving Rising Bills

themes.theme: Bill Forecast to 2035 and Why Cheaper Gas Won't Save Consumers

insights.claim: Absent policy action, BCG's central scenario has nominal UK consumer electricity bills rising £115 (13%) to £996 by 2035, with fixed network costs driving 86% of that increase, even though real (inflation-adjusted) bills actually fall by about 5% over the decade.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/maurice-berns
insights.so_what: Headline nominal bill figures will look alarming through 2035, but the underlying real burden is roughly flat to declining -- useful for separating political narrative from economic reality.
insights.locator: Executive Summary

insights.claim: If GB electricity demand keeps declining at the past decade's pace rather than recovering, bills would be a further £149/year higher by 2035 (15% above the central case) -- demand trajectory is the single largest swing factor in BCG's bill forecast.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/maurice-berns
insights.so_what: Demand growth (or its absence) is the dominant variable for UK household affordability through 2035 -- more decisive than gas prices or generation-mix choices.
insights.locator: Executive Summary

insights.claim: A one-third fall in the wholesale gas price would cut consumer bills by only 3% by 2030 despite wholesale electricity prices falling 17%, because Contracts-for-Difference top-ups claw back roughly a quarter of any wholesale fall and wholesale power is only about a third of a typical bill; the effect is asymmetric, since a wholesale share that shrinks as gas falls also means less relief, while a rising wholesale share as gas rises passes through more fully.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/maurice-berns
insights.so_what: Investors and consumers hoping for gas-price relief to fix UK bills should recalibrate: CfD design has largely decoupled bill relief from further gas-price declines, while still leaving bills exposed to gas price spikes.
insights.locator: Vision of the Future: Higher Fixed Costs Driving Rising Bills

insights.claim: Policy costs and VAT are forecast to stay flat to slightly declining through 2035, a reversal from their large contribution to the historical 2015-24 bill rise, meaning Britain's affordability problem is shifting from being a policy-cost story to a network- and market-design story.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/maurice-berns
insights.so_what: Future bill-relief campaigns focused on scrapping green levies will have a shrinking target -- the real leverage going forward sits in network cost recovery and market design.
insights.locator: Vision of the Future: Higher Fixed Costs Driving Rising Bills

insights.claim: Grid balancing/constraint costs -- paying Scottish wind to curtail output because the network can't carry it south, then paying English gas generation to ramp up instead -- reached £1.7bn in 2024/25, and NESO projects these could rise to as much as £8bn by 2030 if transmission build-out is delayed.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/maurice-berns
insights.so_what: Transmission build delay risk is a direct, quantifiable multi-billion-pound bill risk -- a concrete metric to track UK grid-reinforcement delivery against.
insights.locator: Vision of the Future: Higher Fixed Costs Driving Rising Bills

insights.claim: Non-domestic (industrial) delivered electricity prices rose 131% between 2015 and early 2026, even as industrial electricity demand fell in 2025 to its lowest level since 1983 -- industrial users are being priced out of British power just as heavy industry most needs competitive electricity costs.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/maurice-berns
insights.so_what: UK industrial competitiveness and de-industrialization risk is a live, worsening trend directly tied to electricity pricing, relevant to any UK manufacturing or energy-intensive industry thesis.
insights.locator: Vision of the Future: Higher Fixed Costs Driving Rising Bills

themes.theme: Which Policy Levers Actually Move Bills

insights.claim: Of eight bill-affordability levers BCG tested across four categories (cost allocation, system operation, system build/maintenance, and long-term system shaping), only cost-reallocation and long-term demand-shaping levers have material impact within five to ten years -- operational levers are marginal, with time-of-use tariffs saving only about £6/year and cheaper cost of capital on CfD strike prices saving only about £3/year.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/maurice-berns
insights.so_what: Policy debates focused on operational/tariff tweaks are chasing marginal savings; the two levers worth political capital are cost reallocation and demand growth.
insights.quote: No single lever, on its own, can significantly reduce bills.
insights.locator: Levers to Improve Affordability

insights.claim: BCG's proposed five-lever package could save around £174/year on bills by 2035 versus the central case, but the levers are not simply additive -- because several act on the same underlying cost bases (demand, network revenue, the policy pot), the combined savings come in below the sum of each lever's isolated effect.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/maurice-berns
insights.so_what: Any policymaker or forecaster stacking individual lever estimates to project bill relief will overstate the combined benefit -- BCG's £174 figure should be treated as the credible ceiling.
insights.locator: Executive Summary

insights.claim: Moving legacy social/policy costs -- the Warm Home Discount, and the Renewables Obligation and Feed-in Tariffs for non-domestic users -- onto general taxation could cut domestic bills by £13-17/year and save a small business using 20,000 kWh/year roughly £800/year, at a combined fiscal cost to government of about £5.5 billion/year.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/maurice-berns
insights.so_what: A concrete, costed near-term fiscal ask (~£5.5bn/year) that shifts burden from billpayers to general taxation -- watchable as a specific UK Budget/fiscal-policy lever.
insights.locator: Policies to Improve Near-Term Affordability

insights.claim: Extending network-asset depreciation from the current ~45 years to a more realistic ~55-year technical life could save about £10/year on bills, but slower depreciation weakens network operators' cash-flow ratios and credit ratings, requiring coordination with pension-fund shareholders (who hold most network equity) and possibly government bridging finance.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/maurice-berns
insights.so_what: A regulatory depreciation-schedule change is a low-cost lever but has a direct credit-rating/cost-of-capital tradeoff for network operators -- relevant to anyone holding UK network debt or equity.
insights.locator: Policies to Improve Near-Term Affordability

insights.claim: A National Wealth Fund-style facility could defer capital-related network revenue off bills -- worth up to about £5 billion/year if applied to domestic bills only, or nearly £10 billion/year including non-domestic -- structured as a government loan to networks that nets off public debt if priced at fair value, and recovered from bills later in the asset's life.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/maurice-berns
insights.so_what: A concrete fiscal-engineering mechanism (large enough to matter, £5-10bn/year) that shifts network cost timing rather than eliminating it -- worth tracking as a live UK Treasury/NESO financing proposal.
insights.locator: Policies to Improve Near-Term Affordability

insights.claim: Structural, long-term system-shaping levers such as changing Britain's generation mix cannot move bills within five to ten years because so much of the power system is already financed through committed, sunk fixed costs -- investors and policymakers should not expect near-term bill relief from generation-mix debates.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/maurice-berns
insights.so_what: Tempers expectations that renewables-vs-gas-vs-nuclear policy fights will show up in consumer bills any time soon -- the near-term affordability fight is elsewhere.
insights.locator: Levers to Improve Affordability

insights.claim: Roughly 1.13 million UK consumers are in arrears on their electricity bills, almost double the level of a decade ago, underscoring the urgency behind near-term bill-relief proposals.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/maurice-berns
insights.so_what: A hard, rising energy-poverty metric that strengthens the political case for near-term fiscal intervention and signals consumer-credit/utility-arrears risk.
insights.locator: Policies to Improve Near-Term Affordability

insights.claim: BCG argues that deferring network costs onto future bills is progressive rather than unfair to future generations, since electricity already consumes about 7% of income for the poorest fifth of UK households versus roughly 3% population-wide, and future users will be less price-sensitive with a larger demand base to spread fixed costs across.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/maurice-berns
insights.so_what: Reframes intergenerational cost-shifting debates (often seen as unfair to future taxpayers) as a distributionally progressive tool -- a contrarian argument policymakers may deploy to justify deferral mechanisms.
insights.quote: Electricity has risen to around 7% of income for the poorest fifth
insights.locator: Policies to Improve Near-Term Affordability

insights.claim: British household electricity demand has a long-run price elasticity of about -0.61, versus about -0.82 for industry, meaning industrial electricity demand is meaningfully more price-responsive than domestic demand.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/maurice-berns
insights.so_what: Cheaper power would pull back industrial load, capex, and reshoring decisions faster than it changes household consumption -- relevant for modeling how quickly UK industrial policy could respond to price cuts.
insights.locator: The Key System-Level Lever: Increasing Demand

themes.theme: Data Centres as Britain's Best Demand-Growth Lever

insights.claim: The report's central, counterintuitive policy prescription is that Britain must increase electricity demand, not reduce it, in order to break its negative demand/price spiral -- inverting the conventional 'use less energy' instinct of energy policy.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/maurice-berns
insights.so_what: A direct contrarian framing investors should use to interpret UK energy and data-centre policy: demand growth, not conservation, is being positioned as the fix for consumer bills.
insights.quote: Counterintuitively, the requirement is that Britain use more electricity, not less.
insights.locator: Executive Summary

insights.claim: Data centres are favored over EVs, heat pumps, hydrogen, and other industrial demand as Britain's best demand-growth lever because household consumer demand is inherently constrained, EV/heat-pump growth is already baked into official forecasts, domestic demand mostly represents switching from other fuels rather than net-new demand, and other UK industrial demand sources have been structurally declining for decades.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/maurice-berns
insights.so_what: Frames data centre buildout as economically net-additive in a way EVs/heat pumps are not -- a differentiator for anyone evaluating UK data centre vs. electrification investment theses.
insights.locator: The Key System-Level Lever: Increasing Demand

insights.claim: NESO's committed-financing UK data centre pipeline stands at 20GW, up from 2.4GW installed in 2024; BCG estimates 9-17GW is achievable by 2040 and models 14GW as achievable by 2035 in its upside scenario, benchmarking against Virginia's roughly 1GW/year build rate and Ireland's 20% capacity CAGR from 2019-2023.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/maurice-berns
insights.so_what: Gives investors concrete GW benchmarks (20GW pipeline, 14GW deliverable by 2035) to size the UK data centre power-demand opportunity and compare delivery pace against US/Irish precedent.
insights.locator: The Key System-Level Lever: Increasing Demand

insights.claim: Delivering that 14GW data centre pipeline in a 'grid-positive' way, without requiring significant new generation build, would cut every UK household's electricity bill by about £35/year by 2035, by spreading fixed network costs over a larger usage base.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/maurice-berns
insights.so_what: Directly links AI/data-centre infrastructure buildout to household affordability -- a politically salient number (£35/household) that could anchor UK planning and grid-connection debates.
insights.locator: The Key System-Level Lever: Increasing Demand

insights.claim: Hydrogen electrolysis demand growth (modeled at +12TWh from near zero today) is judged very unlikely given negligible uptake in recent years, in contrast to relatively high confidence in EV demand growth, where the average new electric car became cheaper than the average new petrol car for the first time this year.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/maurice-berns
insights.so_what: A specific skeptical call against the UK hydrogen-economy narrative as a near-term electricity demand source, while flagging EV cost-parity as a genuine, high-confidence demand driver to watch.
insights.locator: The Key System-Level Lever: Increasing Demand

insights.claim: Water availability for data centre cooling is flagged as a potentially material but unassessed constraint on large-scale UK data centre build-out, particularly in areas where local water supply is already constrained.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/maurice-berns
insights.so_what: A second-order risk investors in UK data centre projects should diligence separately, since BCG explicitly did not model it despite calling it out.
insights.locator: The Key System-Level Lever: Increasing Demand

insights.claim: The binding constraint on UK data centre growth is transmission network capacity, not power supply -- renewable generation is growing fastest in Scotland and northern England, while demand is concentrated around London and the South East, where transmission capacity is scarce.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/maurice-berns
insights.so_what: UK data centre siting decisions should weight grid/transmission proximity over raw generation abundance -- explains multi-year connection queues despite ample renewable capacity.
insights.quote: Britain can have abundant generation and still make projects wait years.
insights.locator: The Key System-Level Lever: Increasing Demand

insights.claim: BCG's four-lever 'grid-positive' data centre framework: (1) flexible/non-firm connections with predefined curtailment for loads above 50MW, (2) a national market for 'powered land' (BCG identifies about 18GW of brownfield/ex-power-station sites, roughly 40% with no current redevelopment activity), (3) developer self-build of high-voltage connection assets, and (4) behind-the-meter generation as a bridge or permanent alternative to full grid connection.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/maurice-berns
insights.so_what: A reusable four-part checklist for evaluating whether a UK data centre project (or grid-connection policy) is being designed to add system value rather than just add load.
insights.locator: The Key System-Level Lever: Increasing Demand

insights.claim: Duke University research found that curtailing flexible loads for just about 1% of annual hours (roughly 88 hours) could unlock 126GW of additional load across 22 US balancing areas, about 16.6% of aggregate peak demand -- modest flexibility unlocks large amounts of grid headroom cheaply.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/maurice-berns
insights.so_what: A quantified precedent for how much capacity flexible/curtailable large loads (like data centres) could unlock without new generation -- a benchmark for UK non-firm connection design.
insights.locator: The Key System-Level Lever: Increasing Demand

insights.claim: Non-firm, flexible connection arrangements could cut UK data centre connection times from 5-10 years down to 2-4 years, roughly a 60% reduction, by avoiding or deferring major network reinforcement.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/maurice-berns
insights.so_what: A concrete timeline benefit (60% faster connections) that could materially de-risk UK data centre project schedules if adopted -- worth tracking in Ofgem/NESO connection reform.
insights.locator: The Key System-Level Lever: Increasing Demand

insights.claim: Ireland's contestable self-build model delivered network connections about 20% cheaper and 11 months faster; BCG estimates earlier energisation via self-build could create over $8 million per megawatt in NPV for a data centre operator, and every 1GW of grid-positive capacity could create $1-2 billion in system value from better infrastructure utilization plus $0.5-1 billion from avoided generation and grid reinforcement.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/maurice-berns
insights.so_what: Quantifies the per-MW and per-GW economic upside of self-build connection rights -- a specific value-creation number for data centre developers and system planners to underwrite investment cases against.
insights.locator: The Key System-Level Lever: Increasing Demand

insights.claim: International connection-policy precedents BCG wants Britain to emulate include Texas ERCOT's 'Batch Zero' process for assessing large loads collectively, Virginia's large-load rate class requiring customers to pay at least 85% of the transmission/distribution cost of serving them monthly, and Ireland's rule requiring new data centres to source at least 80% of demand from additional Irish renewables while matching requested capacity with their own generation or storage.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/maurice-berns
insights.so_what: A cross-jurisdiction policy comparison set that signals where UK data centre connection reform is likely headed -- useful for anticipating regulatory requirements (self-supply obligations, cost allocation) in the UK market.
insights.locator: The Key System-Level Lever: Increasing Demand

insights.claim: To avoid the pattern documented in the US where ratepayers subsidize Big Tech's power buildouts, BCG recommends UK large-load connections carry five-to-seven-year minimum-term commitments backed by financial guarantees, so that if a data centre's load fails to materialize, the developer -- not existing billpayers -- bears the stranded cost.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/maurice-berns
insights.so_what: Signals a likely regulatory requirement (multi-year financial guarantees) that data centre developers and their financiers should underwrite into UK project costs and risk models.
insights.quote: make the developer, not existing consumers, bear any incremental costs.
insights.locator: The Key System-Level Lever: Increasing Demand

top_entities: Department for Energy Security and Net Zero (DESNZ)
